implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines gives the pattern as a Flow operator: retry(retries, predicate) re-collects the upstream flow when the predicate matches the exception, and retryWhen(cause, attempt) is the general form that retry delegates to - because the predicate is a suspending function it can also delay, which is how backoff is expressed without a separate policy object (flow.retry(3) { e -> (e is IOException).also { if (it) delay(1000) } }). For a plain suspend function the idiom is to wrap the call in flow { emit(call()) }.retry(...) or to hand-roll a loop with delay(); the operator form therefore fits code that is already flow-shaped (network streams, Flow-based repositories) and the loop remains the honest fallback elsewhere. Either way the delay is a coroutine suspension, not a blocked thread.
code_sketch:
val result = flow { emit(client.fetch()) }        // suspend call as a flow
    .retry(3) { cause -> cause is IOException }    // predicate is suspending
    .catch { emit(cached) }
    .first()
pitfalls: retry is transparent to downstream exceptions and never retries cancellation: catching CancellationException inside the predicate breaks structured concurrency.
The default retries is Long.MAX_VALUE - flow.retry() without arguments retries forever, and the failure only surfaces when the predicate stops matching.
A delay inside the predicate runs per attempt and is not bounded by a total deadline unless a surrounding withTimeout covers the whole collection.
Retrying a flow re-collects it, so upstream side effects (a POST inside the flow builder) happen again on every attempt: the retried unit must be idempotent.

variants.name: kotlin-retry: composable RetryPolicy value with jitter backoffs
variants.idiom_name: retry(policy) { block } with stopAtAttempts + constantDelay + jitter backoffs
variants.implementation_notes: The kotlin-retry library makes the policy a composable value: retry(continueIf<Throwable> { it is SQLDataException } + constantDelay(1000) + stopAtAttempts(5)) { block() } re-invokes a suspending block according to the combined RetryPolicy, with jittered backoff builders (binaryExponentialBackoff, fullJitterBackoff, equalJitterBackoff, decorrelatedJitterBackoff) and a Result-based overload for kotlin-result code. Because the policy is a value it can be built once, shared and unit-tested with virtual time, which is the form to choose when several call sites share one policy or when the delay schedule must follow the published jitter taxonomy rather than a single exponential. The mechanism it replaces is the hand-written while-loop with delay(); the classic loop remains fine for a single call site.
pitfalls: The policy composes with + in a fixed order (continue, delay, stop) and a missing stopAtAttempts means unbounded retrying - always include a stop condition.
retry re-runs the whole block, so work performed before the failing call is repeated; keep the block minimal and idempotent.
Policies are immutable and safe to share, but jitter backoffs draw randomness per attempt: tests need an injected seed or virtual clock to stay deterministic.
Mixing this library with Flow.retry at the same call site multiplies attempts (a policy retry inside an already-retried flow).
